title: Beyond the count: the killing of Indigenous women as a security crisis
gist: The authors argue Indigenous women face a disproportionate global femicide burden that is systematically undercounted by international data systems — the 2024 UN Women-UNODC femicide report (83,000 women and girls killed) makes no mention of Indigenous women specifically — and call for reframing Indigenous femicide as a Women, Peace and Security Agenda priority alongside Indigenous-led, narrative-inclusive evidence-gathering.

themes.theme: Indigenous women's disproportionate, undercounted femicide risk

insights.claim: Indigenous Peoples make up less than 6% of the global population but represent at least 15% of the extremely poor, and violence against Indigenous women and girls often occurs in contexts of extreme vulnerability rooted in racism, structural discrimination, armed conflict, militarisation of Indigenous territories, forced displacement, suppression of cultural practices, and criminalisation of Indigenous women land/environmental defenders.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: A poverty/population disparity statistic (6% vs 15%) that underpins the structural-risk argument for why Indigenous women face compounded femicide vulnerability — relevant context for ESG/human-rights risk screening in extractive and conflict-adjacent regions.
insights.locator: paragraph on Indigenous women's heightened collective risk

insights.claim: The UN Women-UNODC annual femicide report estimates 83,000 women and girls were intentionally killed in 2024, but the report makes no mention of Indigenous women and girls' disproportionate experience of femicide, despite evidence they face a disproportionate and racialised burden.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, named data gap in the flagship global femicide statistic — relevant for any organization funding or relying on UN gender-violence data to know it excludes Indigenous-specific breakdowns.

insights.claim: Indigenous femicide is too often rendered invisible through misclassification, erasure in biased or incomplete data systems, or neglect by authorities, or alternatively made hyper-visible in ways that stigmatise Indigenous communities — a data-system failure the authors attribute to continuing colonial structures determining what is counted and whose experiences are prioritised.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: Frames data infrastructure itself as a mechanism perpetuating the problem — relevant for any policy or philanthropic funder assessing where gaps in Indigenous-disaggregated violence data need investment.
insights.quote: Existing data systems continue to reflect colonial structures that determine what is counted, whose experiences are prioritised, and how violence is interpreted.
insights.locator: paragraph on data systems and colonial structures

themes.theme: Reframing Indigenous femicide as a peace-and-security issue

insights.claim: The authors argue Indigenous femicide is a matter of international peace and security and should be a priority for the UN Women, Peace and Security (WPS) Agenda, noting that the first UN Security Council Resolution on WPS (1325, in 2000) called for measures supporting Indigenous processes for conflict resolution, but there has not been enough progress since then in recognizing Indigenous women's WPS rights to participation, protection, relief and recovery.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: Positions Indigenous femicide within the formal international security-policy architecture (WPS Agenda/UNSCR 1325) rather than purely as a domestic social issue — relevant for tracking how security-policy funding and frameworks may expand to cover this gap.

insights.claim: Australia's recently published mid-term review of its National Action Plan on Women, Peace and Security (2022-32) includes a focus on meaningful First Nations engagement with WPS recommendations, described as a necessary but insufficient step, with the authors calling for much more collaboration, investment and Indigenous-led action across Asia and the Pacific and internationally.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific Australian policy document as an early positive precedent, useful for tracking whether other governments follow with similar First Nations-inclusive WPS commitments.

insights.claim: Statistics alone are insufficient — evidence on Indigenous femicide must be understood broadly to include stories, oral histories, testimonies and community narratives alongside numbers, offering insights into causes, consequences and pathways to healing and prevention that quantitative data systems miss.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: A methodological framework relevant to any research or funding body designing Indigenous violence-data collection: combine quantitative statistics with narrative/oral evidence rather than relying on numbers alone.

insights.claim: Strengthening evidence on Indigenous femicide requires ongoing collaboration about not only improving data but also who owns it, who interprets it, and who benefits from it — a data-sovereignty question the authors say is becoming more urgent as digital technologies and AI expand rapidly.
insights.speaker: Kyllie Cripps
insights.so_what: Flags Indigenous data sovereignty as an emerging governance issue intersecting with AI expansion — relevant for organizations building AI/data systems that touch Indigenous communities' violence or demographic data.
insights.locator: paragraph on data ownership and AI
